text.title: Growth Viral Loops Failure Modes
text.summary: Six antipatterns observed when specifying and running viral loops. Each pairs symptom + root-cause + concrete fix and maps to a rule in 01-core-rules.xml.

antipattern.symptom: The spec quotes a K-factor (0.7, 1.1) but no invites-per-user or accept-rate number exists anywhere; the number came from a benchmark article or a founder's estimate.
antipattern.root-cause: K is treated as an input to the spec instead of an output of instrumentation; nobody has joined invite_sent to invite_accepted.
antipattern.fix: Apply r-k-factor-decomposed: refuse any K that is not shown as i x c with window and sample size. If the events do not exist yet, the spec's first experiment is instrumentation, not incentives.

antipattern.symptom: Every experiment in the spec targets the reward or the invite copy; the projection assumes a 7-day cycle that nobody measured; real invites are accepted a median of 19 days after sending.

root-cause.source: David Skok, Lessons Learned – Viral Marketing

antipattern.root-cause: The team optimises the visible variable (K) and never computed the one that compounds (cycle time).
antipattern.fix: Apply r-cycle-time-measured-and-projected: compute send-to-first-send from timestamps, rerun the projection with the measured value, and add at least one experiment that shortens the cycle (reminder cadence, invite expiry, faster invitee activation).

antipattern.symptom: The "viral loop" is a /refer page linked from the settings menu plus a post-signup modal. invite_shown fires once per user; K measured at 0.02 to 0.05.

root-cause.source: Andrew Chen, The Cold Start Problem (2021)

antipattern.root-cause: No inherent sharing moment was identified; the loop was designed around the incentive rather than around a product action that already involves another person.
antipattern.fix: Apply r-share-moment-is-inherent: map the product's collaborative or outbound actions, pick the one with the highest frequency, and make it the primary loop; demote the referral page to a secondary incentivised loop with its own K.

antipattern.symptom: Referral signups spike, activation of referred users is near zero, the same device fingerprint or payment card appears on dozens of "new" accounts, and finance holds an unexpected credit liability.

root-cause.source: Widely documented referral-program fraud patterns; Dropbox referral design

antipattern.root-cause: The reward trigger was signup, not activation, and no self-referral or per-user cap was defined.
antipattern.fix: Apply r-reward-on-activation-not-signup: move both rewards to the activation milestone within a stated window, cap rewards per referrer per 12 months, block same-device / same-IP / same-card referrals, and exclude past users.

antipattern.symptom: Analytics shows 4,000 invites sent and 900 signups in the same month, so K is reported as 0.22, but no signup can be tied to an invite; the 900 include organic and paid traffic.

root-cause.source: Sean Ellis and Morgan Brown, Hacking Growth (2017)

antipattern.root-cause: Events were named but not keyed: invite_id and inviter user_id are missing, so the funnel is two totals rather than one chain.
antipattern.fix: Apply r-loop-events-instrumented: put invite_id on every event from invite_sent to invitee_activated, carry the inviter's user_id, and compute K and cycle time only from joined rows. Report invitee D30 next to organic D30.

antipattern.symptom: The loop's growth engine is "import your Gmail contacts and we email all of them"; invites carry no compensation disclosure; complaints, spam-flagging and a CASL or GDPR query arrive within the first quarter.

root-cause.source: FTC Endorsement Guides, 16 CFR Part 255; CASL; GDPR Art. 6

antipattern.root-cause: Consent and disclosure were treated as legal afterthoughts rather than as loop design constraints.
antipattern.fix: Apply r-referral-consent-and-disclosure: send only to addresses the inviter enters for that purpose, gate Canadian and EU recipients on consent or lawful basis, add the compensation disclosure to the invite and landing page, and complete the compliance checklist in templates/referral-program.md before launch.

section.title: Human checkpoint
section.p: Before any binding action driven by a Growth Viral Loops output (publish, send, rollout, commit), a named human reviewer must sign off. The agent surfaces a `ready_for_review=true` flag and does NOT auto-commit decisions, copy, configs, or rollouts.
